newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany leans on Airbus after U.S. deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany leans on Airbus after U.S. deal.

text.p: German government and industry officials on Monday pressured their European partners in the Airbus consortium to quickly agree to restructure the aircraft group in the face of heighted American competition.

Plans to create a European aircraft enterprise out of the four-nation Airbus Industrie consortium by 1999 have dragged on because of reluctance by some members to give up control of core development and production capabilities.

But officials in Germany said the planned merger of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas to create a powerhouse with annual turnover of $48 billion made it necessary to transform Airbus into a European counterweight.

"Airbus Industrie and its partners must agree as soon as possible on an optimal structure that will allow Airbus Industrie to match its American competitors as a powerful, integrated European enterprise," German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a statement.

Europe's aerospace industry could not remain idle in the face of Boeing's "monopoly on aircraft with more than 400 seats (B747-Jumbo)". Airbus wants to build its own 500-600 seat jumbo plane and is planning a 100-seater with China and Singapore.
Suggesting that European governments should throw their political weight behind Airbus, Rexrodt said Bonn has actively supported the group since its creation 25 years ago.
"In this business, strongly affected by state influence, the German government will make its contribution in the future to ensure fair competition on the world market," he said.

Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, the world's first and third-largest aircraft makers, at the weekend said they had agreed on a merger valued at $13.3 billion via a stock swap. It must still be approved by U.S. authorities.

Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA), and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.

Boeing is the world leader in civilian aircraft. Where Boeing is strong, McDonnell Douglas has been weakened by the success of the Airbus group. But McDonnell Douglas remains a powerful force in military aircraft. The merger weds the strengths of each company, posing a new challenge to Airbus.

"If Airbus Industrie wants to remain competitive and continue to increase its market share, it must be quickly and courageously restructured by its owners," said German Research and Technology Minister Juergen Ruettgers.
DASA chairman Manfred Bischoff said Airbus must give up its present structure as a partnership and build up a competitive organization integrating design, engineering and manufacturing.
"To do that, it means getting technological advances like our American competitors get them," he told German radio.

Commenting on the continuing debate in Germany over whether to finance development of a European jet fighter, the Eurofighter, a conservative member of parliament said the U.S. aircraft merger made the project more important than ever.

"Without independent European leadership in military aircraft production, civilian aircraft production will fall behind powerful American competition," said Volker Kauder, a member of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats.
